title: Teacher well-being and retention pressure are becoming constraints on sustained public-school capacity
source_unit: RAND State of the American Teacher Survey 2026 and American Life Panel companion survey; nationally representative K–12 public-school teacher panel
geography: United States; K–12 public-school teachers with comparison to employed adults with at least a bachelor’s degree

denominator.unit: weighted responses from nationally representative K–12 public-school teachers

survey_domains.value: well-being, job satisfaction, pay, hours, school climate, student mental-health supports, retention, and teacher background

observations.method: Probability-based American Teacher Panel sample weighted to national K–12 public-school teacher characteristics; companion American Life Panel sample included 498 employed adults ages 18–65 with at least a bachelor’s degree.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is self-reported and cross-sectional in 2026; weighting improves national representation but does not eliminate nonresponse or measurement error, and the companion adults are not a perfect occupational control group.
observations.subgroup: U.S. K–12 public-school teachers, with comparison to employed adults with a bachelor’s degree.
observations.counterinterpretation: Teachers who respond may differ from nonrespondents in stress, retention, or school experience; poor well-being may reflect broader social conditions as well as school working conditions.

poor_wellbeing_relative_to_similar_worke.value: teachers were more likely than similar working adults to report poor well-being on every indicator in 2026, continuing a pattern since 2021

female_teacher_stress_gap.value: female teachers were consistently more likely than male teachers and similar working adults to report frequent job-related stress

wellbeing_constructs.value: job-related stress, coping, depressive symptoms, and burnout

observations.method: Repeated State of the American Teacher survey indicators, including stress, coping, PHQ-2 depressive symptoms, and a four-item burnout operationalization.
observations.uncertainty: These are screening and self-report measures, not clinical diagnoses; repeated survey patterns do not establish that teaching caused the difference or that the same teachers experienced the pattern each year.
observations.subgroup: Public-school teachers, with gender and comparison-worker contrasts reported by RAND.
observations.counterinterpretation: Teachers may differ from comparison workers in age, occupation, schedules, public-facing responsibilities, and reporting norms; gender differences may reflect school, household, or wider labor-market conditions.

intend_to_leave_job.unit: percent of teachers intending to leave their jobs

stay_as_long_as_able.unit: approximately one in four teachers planning to stay in teaching as long as able

outside_job.unit: percent reporting a job outside their school system

outside_job_hours.unit: average hours per week spent in outside jobs among those reporting one

observations.method: Weighted national teacher survey estimates of retention intentions and outside employment.
observations.uncertainty: Intentions are not departures, and outside-job estimates do not identify whether work is financially necessary, chosen for identity or interest, or compatible with teaching quality and rest.
observations.subgroup: U.S. public-school teachers; outside-job hours are conditional on holding an outside job.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some outside work may provide flexibility, professional development, or household resilience; intent-to-leave can change with pay, leadership, school climate, family needs, or labor-market conditions.

denominator.unit: RAND report interpretation connecting teacher working conditions to school service capacity

service_capacity_route.value: teacher stress, financial strain, outside work, and exit intentions can affect staffing continuity, student support, and the ability of schools to sustain learning and mental-health functions

school_work_is_public_infrastructure.value: teacher working conditions have implications for student learning, educator health, engagement, and intentions to stay

observations.method: Synthesis of RAND’s repeated nationally representative teacher surveys and project framing; no causal service-output estimate is claimed.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not measure student outcomes, vacancies, instructional quality, or the causal effect of teacher well-being on school performance.
observations.subgroup: Public-school teachers and the students and schools relying on their continuity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Staffing systems, leadership, curriculum, family conditions, funding, student needs, and local labor markets also shape school capacity; teacher well-being is one route among several.

related_sources.claim: RAND technical documentation and survey results for the 2026 State of the American Teacher Survey.
RAND selected findings report for the 2026 State of the American Teacher survey.
related_sources.access_boundary: RAND’s site returned a 403 during direct retrieval; the RAND project page and technical-documentation metadata were used.

boundary: This record identifies a U.S. public-school workforce trend in which teacher well-being, outside employment, and retention pressure may constrain service continuity. It does not establish clinical prevalence, actual turnover, student achievement effects, or a causal relationship between teacher conditions and school outcomes.
retrieval_hash_scope: Official RAND project page and DOI metadata; direct RAND HTML/PDF retrieval was access-blocked during collection
